changes.before: Define Label with static let prefix = "item:", an instance text property, and static decorate(_:) that prefixes its input. Preserve the input text, including the empty string.
changes.after: Use static for a feature that belongs to the type itself.

before: static makes a member belong to the type rather than one instance. Label.prefix is a shared constant, and Label.decorate is a type function. Each Label still has its own text. A type-wide constant does not mean that all instance properties share one value. We avoid mutable global state in this example.

Label(text:) constructs an instance. Label.decorate(first.text) takes a String and returns a new String with the prefix before it; it does not edit the instance. + joins the two strings. A static function has no particular instance’s text unless one is passed in. Access these static members through Label, not through first.

Follow this complete example.
```swift
struct Label {
    static let prefix = "item:"
    var text: String
    static func decorate(_ text: String) -> String {
        return prefix + text
    }
}
var first = Label(text: "map")
let second = Label(text: "lamp")
first.text = "book"
print(Label.prefix)
print(Label.decorate(first.text))
print(Label.decorate(second.text))
```
Output:
```text
item:
item:book
item:lamp
```

after: A type describes a kind of value. An instance is one value made from that type. static makes a property or function belong to the type itself. Here, Label has one fixed prefix, while each label has its own text.
Use Label.prefix to read the type's prefix. Use Label.decorate(...) to put it before some text. Pass the text in: a static function has no particular label's text of its own.
static applies only to the feature marked with it. It does not make every property shared. decorate joins the prefix and the supplied text, returning a new string without editing either label.
